chapter: Portraits from Hemphill to Getz, and the bebop question
title: Visiting Duke's band in Chicago and watching his men swing
summary: Duke introduced Horace and 'the angelic' wife from the stage while his men wandered off; at a State Street concert Horace's own band swayed with Duke's sections.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Ray is quite a guy. I went to see Ray when he was playing with Duke either in Chicago -- it had to be Chicago. (Inaudible) I had my wife with me at this particular time. Duke was playing in a theater there in Chicago, and they were on stage. And when they walked down almost to the stage, which my wife likes to sit near the band, look at all the guys. I like to sit back where I can hear them. But nevertheless we sat down pretty close. Duke could see us. And I saw Ray get off the bandstand and while the band was swinging, playing -- and went somewhere else and come back. Then I saw another guy get off, one of those things. I found out later the guy was just like Fletcher, you know, he wouldn't reprimand them. He would leave them on their own; they'd take advantage of that. But they would play for him, you know, and this particular time that I was speaking about Duke saw us, and he acknowledged us, which I thought was a great thing, and everything, and he said, 'Fellows, come and say hello to Horace Henderson.' (Inaudible) got right, on the stand, the stage and bowed, and he said, 'We want you to say hello to his lovely wife, the angelic one.' (Inaudible) They kind of got up and bowed. In unison, Impressive, you know? And it was a funny thing. And I could tell those guys, you know, were having fun and all these things.

And speaking of Duke, while we're talking about the band, he played a concert at one of the -- I don't know if it was an auditorium or where -- in Chicago, on State Street. I can't think. It's a place where they used to have these marathon --

-- (inaudible) and whatnot. And they've got a balcony upstairs, and the reason I'm going to mention this is because I had a band at that time, and they always idolized Duke's kind of liked this band. We were upstairs. And that band was playing a riff -- I don't know what it was. An arrangement, I should say. And I stood -- I had to turn around and look at my band when these guys were swinging.

We were looking down on them. And Duke had a thing going on the out chorus (inaudible) where the brass had a little corner and the saxophones had one going. When I said the brass I meant the trumpets.

And the trombones had another little one going corner, and the saxophones -- and my musicians they were ? heads just going like this; you're in the way. They were looking they didn't know where. They were looking down; there. (Inaudible) where Duke was standing in front, waving, you know, and they were swinging! I don't know what the tune was. But these guys' necks were moving with every movement of that, and it was the funniest thing. If I could

have taken a picture, it would have been a classic. But Duke was swinging, and I never will forget that. Of course, Ray was in that band. This is the band I'm talking about : Procope (Unaudible). Krupa was there. It was one of those big, huge auditoriums there in Chicago. I can't think remember the name, but it was down on State Street, where they had those marathon contests.
So that's a story on Ray Nance.
